Battery & Pressure Testing

A watch battery is never just a battery. Every replacement at It's About Time includes a full pressure test and gasket inspection, so your timepiece leaves as water-resistant as the day it was sealed.

From $35 Most done same day Walk-ins welcome
Start a Repair Call the shop

What's included

Every battery service, done properly.

Genuine cell replacement

Swiss-grade silver-oxide cells matched to your calibre, fitted under magnification.

Full pressure test

Dry and wet testing to your watch's rated depth confirms the seal before it leaves the bench.

New gaskets & seals

Case-back and crown gaskets inspected and replaced as needed, then freshly lubricated.

Function check

Date, chronograph, and end-of-life indicators verified so nothing surprises you later.

How it works

In and out, often within the hour.

01

Bring it in

Walk in or send it insured. No appointment needed for battery work.

02

Open & inspect

The case is opened under magnification and the movement and seals assessed.

03

Replace & seal

Fresh cell and gaskets fitted, then the case is closed to factory torque.

04

Pressure test

Water resistance confirmed and the reading noted before it's handed back.

Why it matters

A new battery breaks the seal. We put it back.

Opening a case exposes the movement to air, dust, and moisture. Most jewelers snap the back on and hand it over. Without a fresh gasket and a pressure test, a watch rated for the pool can fail at the sink.

That's why pressure testing is standard here, never an upsell. You leave knowing exactly how water-resistant your watch is today, not how it was rated years ago.

  • Dry and wet testing on every water-resistant watch
  • Documented reading you can keep on file
  • Backed by our service guarantee

Fair, flat, and quoted up front.

Final pricing depends on your calibre and water-resistance rating. You'll always approve it before we begin.

Questions

Good to know before you come in.

Do I need an appointment?+

No. Battery and pressure testing are walk-in services. Most standard replacements are finished while you wait; water-resistant and screw-down cases may need a day for a full test cycle.

Why does a pressure test cost extra?+

The test itself uses specialist equipment and a full cycle of dry and wet measurement. A plain battery swap on a non-water-resistant dress watch doesn't require it, so we don't charge for what your watch doesn't need.

Can you service Rolex and other luxury quartz?+

Yes. Our watchmakers are WOSTEP certified and hold brand authorizations. Screw-down and specialist cases are opened with the correct tooling and resealed to factory specification.

What if my watch still won't run?+

If a fresh cell doesn't bring it back, the movement likely needs service. We'll diagnose it on the spot and credit the battery toward a full overhaul if you choose to proceed.

Written by the Workshop Team

Exploring the Legacy and Craftsmanship of Benrus Watches

Benrus is one of the most storied names in American watchmaking, a brand whose military service, mid-century design, and enduring collectibility have made it a favorite among enthusiasts and first-time buyers alike.

Key Takeaways

  • Founded in 1921, Benrus rose to become a top-tier American brand by the 1950s before falling quiet in the mid-1970s.
  • Its military watches — the Type I and Type II dive watches and DTU-2A/P field watch — are the most sought-after pieces today.
  • Vintage Benrus typically trades between $300 and $1,500, with rare military and asymmetric-case models commanding far more.
  • Always verify condition, originality, and movement authenticity — ideally with a watchmaker — before buying vintage.

Benrus is one of those names that carries a certain weight among watch collectors. For some, it recalls a childhood watch handed down through a family. For others, it evokes the black-dialed field and dive watches that saw service on the wrists of American soldiers. Whichever way you first encounter the brand, the same thing tends to happen: what starts as passing curiosity turns into a genuine appreciation for the craft.

Yet for all its history, Benrus is easy to misunderstand. It sits in the sweet spot between disposable fashion watches and untouchable luxury, which is exactly why it rewards a closer look. This is a guide to where the brand came from, why its watches matter, and what to know before you buy, collect, or restore one.

A Century of Benrus: A Journey Through Time

The Benrus story begins in 1921, when Benjamin Lazrus founded the company in New York City. Like many watch firms of the era, it started small, assembling and casing movements sourced largely from Switzerland. What set Benrus apart was ambition. Within a few decades it had grown from a modest operation into one of the most recognizable watch brands in the United States.

The Rise to Prominence

By the 1950s, Benrus had earned a place among the best-selling watch brands in America, competing directly with names like Bulova, Elgin, and Hamilton. Much of that success came from a clear-eyed understanding of its audience: well-made, attractive watches priced within reach of ordinary buyers. Benrus was never trying to be the most expensive watch on the wrist — it aimed to be the most watch for the money, and for a long stretch it delivered exactly that.

Innovation and Patents

Benrus was not content simply to case other people's movements. Over the years the company filed a steady stream of patents with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, covering everything from case construction to movement refinements. That willingness to invest in engineering, rather than just marketing, is a large part of why vintage Benrus pieces still feel considered and well-built decades later.

Benrus in the Military: Watches That Served

If there is one corner of Benrus history that matters most to collectors today, it is the military chapter. Benrus supplied timepieces to the U.S. armed forces across multiple generations of service, from the Second World War through Vietnam. These weren't dress watches. They were tools, built to a government specification and expected to survive conditions that would end an ordinary watch.

Military Contracts and Specifications

Benrus military watches were produced against strict U.S. military specifications — documents like MIL-W-3818 for field watches and MIL-W-50717 for the asymmetric-cased dive watches. These specifications dictated everything from case construction and legibility to luminous material and shock resistance. The result is a level of consistency and ruggedness that makes surviving examples genuinely collectible.

Authenticating Military Models

Authenticity is everything with military Benrus, and the details are what separate a real piece from a reproduction or a "franken" watch assembled from mismatched parts. Case-back engravings, contract stamps, and the MIL-spec designation are the first things to check, and they should be consistent with each other and with the model's known production window.

  • Cross-check case-back contract numbers and inspection stamps.
  • Verify dial, hands, and lume against documented references.
  • Confirm the movement is the correct caliber for the model and period.
  • Cross-reference the MIL-spec designation against the known production range.

If a seller can't speak to these details, or hasn't documented them, treat that as a reason to slow down, not an outright deal-breaker. Even a genuine military Benrus is worth verifying before money changes hands.

Collecting Vintage Benrus: A Guide for Enthusiasts

The vintage watch market rewards patience and knowledge, and Benrus is no exception. Because the brand sits below the luxury tier, it is often possible to acquire a genuinely interesting piece of watchmaking history for a fraction of what a comparable "name" brand would cost — provided you know what you're looking at.

Model Identification and Valuation

Identifying a specific Benrus model begins with the case back. Most examples carry a model reference number stamped inside, which can be matched against collector catalogs and online databases. From there, design, case shape, dial layout, and movement caliber all help narrow down exactly what you're holding. Valuation follows condition and originality: an all-original, unpolished example with its correct dial and movement will always command more than a restored or modified one.

Common Pitfalls When Buying Vintage

The vintage market can be unforgiving to the impatient buyer. Most of the common regrets we hear come down to the same handful of avoidable mistakes, so it's worth keeping them in mind before you commit.

⚠ Common Pitfalls to Avoid

  • Buying without verifying the watch is in working condition.
  • Overlooking signs of a botched or non-original replacement part.
  • Trusting online seller descriptions without independent verification.
  • Overpaying for a rare-looking piece that hasn't been inspected.
  • Skipping a second-opinion assessment by a qualified watchmaker.

Thinking of buying vintage?

Have any Benrus authenticated before you buy.

Bring a piece to the bench, or send photos ahead, and a certified watchmaker will check originality, condition, and movement before you commit.

Talk to a Watchmaker

Modern Benrus: Bridging Heritage and Innovation

The Benrus name went quiet in the mid-1970s, but the story didn't end there. In more recent years the brand has been revived, with the trademark changing hands and new custodians working to reintroduce it to a contemporary audience. Understanding what the revived brand represents, and how it differs from the vintage pieces, matters if you're deciding between the two.

New Models and Their Appeal

Contemporary Benrus watches are designed to appeal to buyers who appreciate the brand's story but want a modern, warrantied watch on the wrist. The new models typically lean into Benrus's most recognizable heritage designs — the asymmetric-cased dive watch above all — while updating materials, water resistance, and reliability for present-day wear.

✓ Potential Advantages of Modern Benrus

  • A brand-new watch with full manufacturer warranty and no restoration risk.
  • Modern reliability, improved water resistance, and updated materials.
  • Heritage-inspired design without the fragility of a decades-old movement.
  • Readily available to buy new, rather than hunted down on the vintage market.
  • A lower barrier to entry into the Benrus name for first-time buyers.

Challenges and Opportunities

A revived brand always faces the same balancing act: honoring its history without pretending to be something it isn't. For collectors, the modern watches will never carry the provenance of a period military piece, and that's simply the nature of a relaunched marque. But for the buyer who wants the look and spirit of a Benrus without the risks of vintage ownership, the current offerings fill a real and useful gap. The two eras don't compete so much as serve different buyers at different points on the same journey.

“

A Benrus rarely announces itself, and that's exactly its charm — genuine watchmaking history, at a price that still leaves room to actually wear it.

It's About Time Workshop Team

Buying, Servicing, and Caring for a Benrus

Whether you already own a Benrus or are considering one, the practical side matters just as much as the history. Vintage examples in particular need a watchmaker who understands older, often American, movements and can source or fabricate parts that are no longer manufactured. A routine service on a healthy vintage Benrus is usually straightforward; a neglected one that has sat unrun for decades can be a larger undertaking.

Our advice is always the same: have any vintage piece assessed before you rely on it, and set a realistic budget for bringing it back to correct running order. A watch that has been properly serviced will not only keep better time, it will protect the value of an increasingly collectible name.

Have Your Benrus Assessed & Serviced

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the history of Benrus watches?+

Benrus was founded in 1921 by Benjamin Lazrus in New York City and grew into one of the top American watch brands by the 1950s. The company supplied field and dive watches to the U.S. military through several decades before falling quiet in the mid-1970s. The name has since been revived under new ownership.

Are Benrus watches worth anything today?+

Yes. Everyday vintage models often trade between roughly $300 and $1,500, while original military-issue pieces — especially the Type I and Type II dive watches — can command significantly more at auction. Condition, originality, and provenance drive the value.

How do I identify a vintage Benrus watch model?+

Start with the case back, which usually carries a model reference number you can match against collector catalogs and databases. Dial layout, case shape, and movement caliber help confirm it. When in doubt, a watchmaker experienced with vintage Benrus can identify the piece and flag any non-original parts.

Where can I buy a Benrus watch?+

Vintage Benrus turns up with specialist dealers, at auction, and through online marketplaces. Buy from sellers who document condition and originality. New, warrantied models are available directly from the revived Benrus brand. Either way, an in-person or expert inspection is worth the effort.

What are Benrus military watches, and why are they collectible?+

These are watches Benrus produced against U.S. military specifications for service use, including field watches and the asymmetric-cased Type I and Type II dive watches. Relatively low production, genuine field history, and strict build standards make surviving, original examples highly sought after.

How do I find replacement parts or get a Benrus watch repaired?+

Because many parts are no longer manufactured, vintage Benrus repair calls for a watchmaker experienced with older movements who can source period-correct components or carefully fabricate them. A qualified independent workshop is usually your best option — and the right first step is a diagnostic assessment.

Is getting a Benrus watch repaired going to be expensive?+

It depends entirely on the movement's condition. A routine service on a healthy vintage Benrus is reasonable, while a piece that has sat unrun for years, or needs fabricated parts, costs more. We always provide a written estimate before any work begins, so there are no surprises.

Trust Your Benrus to a Specialist

Not every jeweler is equipped to work on a vintage American movement, and a Benrus — particularly a military model — deserves someone who understands what makes it original and what doesn't. The wrong parts or an over-polished case can quietly erase both character and value.

At It's About Time, we assess, service, and restore vintage pieces the right way: original where possible, honest about what we find, and always with a written estimate before we touch anything. Whether you've just inherited a Benrus, are weighing a purchase, or want a cherished piece brought back to correct running order, come visit us in Johns Creek or call to speak with a certified watchmaker.

5 Signs Your Bulova Watch Needs Repair

A Bulova is built to last, but it will tell you when something's wrong long before it stops for good, if you know what to look, listen, and feel for.

Key Takeaways

  • A watch losing more than 15–30 seconds a day is telling you something before it stops entirely.
  • Fogging or condensation under the crystal means water is already inside — stop wearing it and bring it in.
  • Grinding or scraping noises are never normal — take it off your wrist immediately.
  • Most quartz batteries should be replaced every 1–2 years, before they leak and corrode the movement.

Bulova has been making watches for more than 140 years. They're built to last, but even a well-made timepiece will show signs of wear over time. Regular use, environmental exposure, and aging components all take a toll.

Most of the Bulovas that come across our bench weren't dropped or abused. They were simply worn, day after day, for years, and the small warning signs that showed up along the way went unnoticed until the watch stopped running entirely. That's usually the more expensive outcome. A watch that's diagnosed early is often a $35 fix. The same issue ignored for a year can turn into a full movement overhaul.

Spotting problems early matters, and it's easier than most people think once you know what to look, listen, and feel for. Here's a closer look at the five signs we see most often, what's actually happening inside the case, and when it's worth bringing your watch in.

Quartz vs. Mechanical: Different Watches, Different Warning Signs

The first thing worth knowing is that what's actually wrong depends heavily on which type of movement is inside your case.

Battery-powered

Quartz Movements

A weak or dying battery is the most common cause of erratic timing. Corroded contacts and leaking old batteries can also damage surrounding components.

Self-winding

Mechanical Movements

Dried lubricants, worn components, and magnetization from phones or magnetic clasps are the usual culprits. Demagnetizing is often a quick, inexpensive fix.

1. Inaccurate Timekeeping

The most basic job of any watch is to keep accurate time, so it's usually the first thing people notice. If your Bulova is running fast, slow, or stopping without explanation, that's a clear signal something is wrong, even if the watch still looks and feels fine on the wrist.

Accuracy tolerances vary by movement type, and it helps to know what's normal before deciding what's not. Most Bulova quartz watches should stay within about 15 seconds a month. Standard mechanical models typically run within 20 to 30 seconds a day, which sounds like a lot until you remember that's a full day's drift. If you own a Bulova Precisionist, the tolerance is far tighter, often within 10 seconds a year, so even a small deviation is worth investigating on those models specifically.

For quartz models, a weak or dying battery is by far the most common cause. As the battery drains, the movement can't maintain consistent power output, and that shows up as erratic timekeeping before the watch stops altogether. It's worth checking when the battery was last replaced before assuming anything more serious is going on.

For mechanical models, the usual culprits are dried lubricants, worn components, or magnetization. This last one surprises people: everyday items like smartphones, tablet covers, and magnetic bag clasps can magnetize a movement over time, disrupting the balance wheel and escapement in ways that mimic more serious damage. The good news is that demagnetizing is quick and inexpensive, often just a few minutes on the right equipment. If that's ruled out and the timing issue persists, a full service is likely the next step.

2. Water Damage or Fogging

Moisture inside the case is, in our experience, the single most damaging thing that can happen to a watch, and it's also one of the easiest to catch early if you're paying attention. If you see condensation under the crystal, foggy glass that won't clear on its own, or faint water spots through a transparent case back, treat it as urgent rather than cosmetic.

Water ingress corrodes metal components, stains the dial, and, given enough time, damages the movement itself. The longer moisture sits inside a sealed case, the worse and more expensive the eventual repair becomes. We've seen watches that came in a week after the fogging appeared and needed nothing more than a battery and a fresh gasket. We've also seen ones that sat for months and needed a full movement rebuild.

Sometimes the damage isn't visible at all. If your watch was splashed or submerged and then started running erratically, or stopped altogether, moisture may already be inside even without any fogging you can see. That's part of why we treat "it got wet" as reason enough to bring a watch in, regardless of how it looks.

Water resistance ratings are tested under controlled, factory-fresh conditions, and they degrade over time as gaskets and seals dry out, crack, and lose effectiveness, especially with heat exposure. Hot showers, saunas, and hot tubs are particularly hard on seals, since the rapid temperature swings cause them to expand and contract repeatedly. Even a watch rated for real water resistance is worth testing periodically if you wear it anywhere near water.

3. Power Reserve Issues

Automatic Bulova watches wind through the natural movement of your wrist and store that energy in the mainspring. Quartz models simply run on battery power. When either type stops holding a charge the way it should, there's an underlying cause worth chasing down rather than living with.

A healthy automatic Bulova typically offers somewhere between 38 and 48 hours of power reserve when fully wound, though the exact number varies by model. Quartz models should run reliably right up until the battery is nearly depleted. Many Bulova quartz movements will actually tell you this is happening: the second hand starts moving in four-second jumps instead of a smooth one-second tick, a built-in low-battery signal on many, though not all, of their models.

In automatic watches, a worn or loose rotor is a common cause of reduced reserve. If the weighted rotor that spins with your wrist isn't engaging the winding mechanism properly, the mainspring simply never stores enough energy, and the watch runs down faster than it should even with regular wear. In quartz models, a depleted battery is the obvious first check, but corroded battery contacts or a failing electronic module can also interrupt power delivery. Batteries left in too long sometimes leak, and that corrosion tends to spread to surrounding components, turning a $30 fix into something considerably more involved.

As a rule of thumb, we recommend replacing a quartz Bulova's battery every one to two years rather than waiting for the watch to stop completely. If you own a Bulova solar or light-powered model, none of this applies in quite the same way, since those charge from ambient light and have different maintenance needs entirely.

4. Physical Damage or Loose Parts

Not all physical damage is equally urgent, and it's worth knowing the difference between what's purely cosmetic and what actually needs attention right away.

Urgent issues include a cracked or chipped crystal, a loose or stiff crown, loose hands rattling inside the dial, or any visible gap in the case back. Each of these compromises the watch's ability to keep out water, dust, and debris, and left alone, they tend to lead to movement damage down the line. Non-urgent, purely cosmetic issues, like surface scratches on the case or bracelet, don't affect how the watch runs. A skilled watchmaker can polish those out, but there's no rush.

A simple visual check goes a long way. Look for chips or cracks in the crystal, dents in the case, and any play in the crown when it's pushed all the way in. Give the watch a gentle shake and listen for rattling, which can signal a loose hand, a detached component, or debris that's found its way inside. Check the case back for gaps too, especially if the watch has been dropped or knocked against something hard recently.

For most Bulova models, repairing physical damage is worth the cost, particularly for pieces with sentimental or collector value. Crystal replacement in particular is often more affordable than people expect, and it restores both function and appearance in one visit.

5. Unusual Noises or Grinding Sounds

Mechanical watches make noise, and that's normal. The steady tick of an escapement and the soft, faint spin of an automatic rotor are both part of how the watch is supposed to sound. What isn't normal is grinding, scraping, or a harsh rattle that wasn't there before.

These sounds usually mean metal parts are contacting each other in ways they shouldn't, or that debris has found its way into the movement. Left alone, this kind of wear compounds quickly and can cause damage that's difficult, or impossible, to reverse.

Dried or degraded lubricant is the most common cause. Watch oils break down over years of use, and once they lose their protective properties, friction between moving parts increases. You might notice this first as a subtle grinding or roughness in the winding action, well before it becomes a sound you can hear without holding the watch to your ear. Debris is the other common cause, dust, lint, and tiny metal particles accumulating inside the movement over time and interfering with the escapement, especially in older watches that haven't been serviced in many years.

If you hear grinding or scraping, our advice is simple: stop wearing the watch immediately. Continued use risks turning a fixable problem into permanent damage. Bring it in for a diagnosis as soon as you reasonably can.

The 5 Signs at a Glance

If you're skimming rather than reading start to finish, here's the short version of everything above.

Sign What You'll Notice What to Do
Inaccurate TimekeepingRuns fast, slow, or stops intermittentlyCheck battery or wind level; see a watchmaker if unresolved
Water Damage or FoggingCondensation under crystal, rust, or discolorationSeek professional inspection immediately
Power Reserve IssuesWatch stops prematurely or drains too fastReplace battery or service winding mechanism
Physical Damage or Loose PartsCracked crystal, loose crown, rattling soundsHave a watchmaker assess urgency and repair
Unusual Noises or GrindingGrinding, scraping, or rattling from insideStop wearing and take to a repair center right away

"A dead battery left in the case doesn't just stop the watch, it can leak and cause corrosion that costs far more to fix than a routine swap."

— It's About Time Workshop Team

How Urgent Is Each Sign?

Not every symptom means drop everything, but a few genuinely can't wait.

1
Inaccurate timekeepingRoutine

Check the battery age first. If timing drifts persist after a fresh battery, it's worth a bench visit.

2
Water damage or foggingUrgent

Moisture inside the case corrodes components fast. The longer it sits, the more expensive the repair.

3
Power reserve issuesMonitor

A worn rotor or aging battery rarely fails overnight, but it won't fix itself either.

4
Cracked crystal or loose crownUrgent

These compromise the seal against water, dust, and debris. Surface scratches, by contrast, are purely cosmetic.

5
Grinding or scraping noisesCritical

Metal contacting metal inside the movement. Stop wearing it immediately and bring it in.

Learn About Our Battery & Pressure Testing Service

What Happens During a Repair Assessment?

The process is methodical and typically takes only a few minutes once your watch is with the technician, but each step serves a specific purpose.

01
Visual inspection

The case and crystal are checked for cracks, fogging, or damage that could hint at what's wrong before it's even opened.

02
Timing test

The movement is measured against a calibrated reference to see how far off it's actually running.

03
Water resistance check

If fogging or moisture is suspected, a pressure test confirms whether the seals are still doing their job.

04
Movement diagnosis

The case is opened under magnification to check for worn lubricant, magnetization, or physical wear.

05
Estimate & approval

You'll get a written estimate before any work begins, and nothing proceeds without your sign-off.

Watch Owner's Newsletter

Get our monthly watch care guides and service reminders. No spam, unsubscribe anytime.

What Happens If You Ignore These Signs?

The short answer: moisture, wear, and dried lubricant don't get better on their own, they compound. A watch is a closed environment, and once something is wrong inside it, it tends to stay wrong until someone opens the case and fixes it.

A small amount of water inside the case can cause corrosion on the movement parts, rust on the mainspring, and staining on the dial that's often impossible to fully reverse. The condensation you see under the crystal today is frequently just the visible tip of a problem that's already a full movement service away from being a simple fix. The same is true of grinding sounds: what starts as dried lubricant on one pivot can, over months of continued wear, scar a jewel or bend a delicate part that would have cost nothing to avoid.

None of this is meant to be alarming. Watches are remarkably forgiving machines, and almost everything on this list is fixable, often for less than people expect. The point is simply that time works against you here in a way it doesn't with most other things you own.

⚠ The cost comparison: A pre-emptive battery swap or gasket replacement typically runs $35–$65. A movement damaged by unresolved water exposure can run $200–$500 or more, depending on how long the moisture sat inside.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should I service my Bulova watch?+

Mechanical Bulova watches generally benefit from a full service every 3 to 5 years, including cleaning, fresh lubrication, and movement adjustment. Quartz models need less frequent attention but should have the battery replaced every 1 to 2 years.

Does a battery replacement void my watch's water resistance?+

Not on its own, but opening the case does reset your water resistance to unknown until it's pressure tested again. That's why a proper battery service always includes a fresh gasket and a test.

Can I repair my Bulova watch at home?+

Basic tasks like swapping a leather strap or cleaning the case exterior are fine at home. Anything involving the movement, crystal, crown, or case seals should go to a professional.

How much does Bulova watch repair cost?+

A battery replacement typically runs $20 to $50. Crystal replacement and seal work generally fall in the $75 to $150 range. A complete movement overhaul can range from $200 to $500 or more depending on complexity.

What happens if my watch fails a pressure test?+

A failed test usually means a worn gasket or seal, an easy and inexpensive fix if caught early. We'll always quote replacement before doing any work, and check for internal moisture at the same time.

Where to Get a Bulova Watch Repaired

Not every jeweler or watch shop has the right equipment. A proper diagnosis requires a calibrated timing machine, and the results are only meaningful if the technician knows how to interpret them and replace gaskets correctly.

Your best options are an authorized service center for your brand, or a qualified independent watchmaker. When you call ahead, ask two things: whether they perform testing as part of a battery or service visit, and whether they replace gaskets at the same time. If the answer to either is no, it's worth finding a shop that does.

At It's About Time, pressure testing is part of how we approach any service that involves opening the case. It's never an add-on, it's just the right way to do the job. Whether it's a $35 battery swap or a full mechanical overhaul, you'll get a written estimate before we touch anything, and you'll get a real explanation of what we found and why. Come visit us in Johns Creek or call to speak with a certified watchmaker.

Dial Refinishing vs. Dial Replacement: How to Know Which One Your Watch Needs

Your watch dial is the first thing you see every time you check the time. When it starts showing signs of wear, fading, or damage, the question is straightforward: can it be restored, or does it need to be replaced? The answer depends on the type of damage, the watch itself, and what you want to preserve.

Key Takeaways

  • Dial refinishing restores the existing dial surface without replacing it. It works best for fading, discoloration, light scratches, and worn printing.
  • Dial replacement swaps the original dial for a new one. It is typically necessary when there is structural damage, severe corrosion, or irreparable water damage.
  • For vintage or collectible watches, keeping the original dial — even in imperfect condition — almost always preserves more value than refinishing or replacing it.
  • A qualified watchmaker should inspect the dial in person before recommending either option. The right answer depends on the watch, its history, and your goals.

What Is Watch Dial Refinishing?

Watch dial refinishing is the process of restoring a dial's original appearance by stripping, recoating, and reprinting the existing dial surface without replacing it.

A skilled technician strips the existing finish down to the base metal, applies a new surface coating to match the original color and texture, reprints any text or branding using a plate made from the original design, and reapplies luminous material to the markers if applicable.

The result, when done well, is a dial that looks close to its original factory condition. The key phrase is "when done well." Dial refinishing is a specialized craft that requires precise equipment, correct font libraries, and experience with specific finishes. Not every watchmaker offers this service, and not every shop that offers it does it at the level a luxury watch demands.

Pro Tip

If your watchmaker cannot show you examples of previous dial refinishing work on a similar brand or dial type, that is a strong signal to look elsewhere. Refinishing a sunburst Omega dial and refinishing a matte Rolex dial are very different jobs.

What Is Watch Dial Replacement?

Watch dial replacement is the complete removal of the original dial and installation of a new, compatible dial in its place.

The replacement dial must be compatible with the watch's movement, meaning the dial feet position, center hole diameter, and date window alignment all need to match precisely.

For luxury watches, the replacement dial should be a genuine manufacturer-sourced part. Aftermarket dials exist, but installing one on a luxury timepiece can compromise its authenticity, void manufacturer warranties, and reduce resale value. Rolex, for example, states in its warranty policy that coverage does not apply to watches modified with non-genuine parts or components, including dials.

Replacement is the more invasive option. It gives you a factory-fresh look, but you lose the original dial permanently.

Dial Refinishing vs. Dial Replacement: Side-by-Side Comparison

The table below breaks down the key differences between refinishing and replacement to help you quickly identify which option fits your situation.

Factor Dial Refinishing Dial Replacement
What it doesRestores the existing dial surfaceRemoves the old dial and installs a new one
Best forFading, discoloration, light scratches, worn printingSevere corrosion, structural cracks, irreparable water damage
Original dial retained?Yes (modified)No (replaced entirely)
Impact on vintage/collectible valueCan reduce value if originality is a priorityAlmost always reduces value for collectible pieces
Impact on daily-wear watchesOften the best balance of appearance and costCan be worthwhile when the dial is beyond refinishing
TurnaroundOften 2 to 4 weeks, but varies by shop, dial complexity, and whether work is in-house or outsourcedVaries by parts availability; manufacturer-sourced dials may take longer
Risk if done poorlyMismatched fonts, color inconsistency, reduced valueIncompatible dial feet, date misalignment, loss of authenticity

When Refinishing Is the Right Call

Refinishing makes sense when the dial's structure is intact but the surface has deteriorated. Common scenarios include:

Faded or discolored dial: Sun exposure over years can bleach colors and dull printed text. If the underlying metal is in good shape, refinishing can bring the dial back to its original appearance.

Worn or flaking printing: Brand logos, hour markers, and minute tracks can wear away over time. A refinishing specialist creates a printing plate from the original design and reapplies the text and markings.

Light surface scratches: Superficial marks on the dial surface that do not penetrate the base metal can often be corrected during the refinishing process.

Luminous material has degraded: Older watches frequently need their lume reapplied. This is typically done as part of a refinishing job when the original luminous paint has crumbled or discolored.

When Replacement Is the Better Option

Some damage goes beyond what refinishing can correct. Replacement is typically the better path when:

⚠ Damage Refinishing Cannot Fix

  • Water has corroded the dial: Moisture inside the case can cause oxidation, pitting, and rust that eats into the base metal. If the dial surface is bubbled, warped, or structurally compromised, refinishing cannot restore it safely.
  • Dial is cracked or bent: Physical impact that deforms or fractures the dial makes refinishing impractical. The base must be structurally sound for any surface treatment to hold.
  • Markers or indices are missing: Applied markers that have fallen off may be difficult or impossible to source individually. In some cases, a new dial with factory-installed markers is the cleaner solution.
  • Previous refinishing was done poorly: If an earlier job used incorrect fonts, wrong colors, or misaligned printing, starting fresh with a genuine replacement dial may be preferable to correcting someone else's work.

Pro Tip

If your watch stopped working and you suspect water entered the case, do not wait. Corrosion starts immediately and can damage both the dial and the movement within days. Bring the watch in for inspection as soon as possible. At It's About Time Inc., we diagnose dial, crystal, and crown issues before recommending any service.

Not sure which you need?

Refinish or Replace?

Bring your watch to It's About Time Inc. for a professional inspection. We diagnose before we recommend, and we will explain your options clearly before any work begins.

Start a Repair Form

The Vintage Watch Question: Should You Touch the Dial at All?

This is where the decision gets more nuanced. In the collector market, the original dial is widely considered the most valuable single component of a vintage watch. Industry experts and auction specialists have noted that a watch with original parts, especially the dial, often commands significantly higher value than one with replacements. Some vintage watch appraisers estimate that the dial accounts for the majority of a collectible watch's value.

The general guidance among experienced watchmakers and collectors is straightforward: if the dial is legible and structurally sound, leave it alone. Patina, which includes the natural aging and discoloration that develops over decades, is increasingly seen as desirable rather than something to fix. In certain collector segments, patina actively increases value. Vintage Rolex Submariners with "tropical" dials, where the original black has faded to warm brown tones over decades, routinely command premiums of $30,000 to $100,000 or more at major auction houses like Phillips, Christie's, and Sotheby's. That premium exists specifically because the dial was never refinished or replaced.

It is worth noting that this guidance reflects collector market norms rather than a universal rule. The specific model, era, condition, and buyer pool all influence whether originality carries a premium for any given watch.

That said, not every vintage watch is a collector's item. If the watch is a personal timepiece you wear daily and the dial's condition bothers you, refinishing or replacement is a valid choice. The key is making that decision with full awareness of the tradeoff.

If you own a vintage piece and are weighing your options, our guide to collecting and caring for vintage watches covers the broader restoration decisions in detail.

What Affects the Cost?

Several factors influence what you will pay for either service:

Dial Complexity

A simple single-color dial with printed indices costs less to refinish than a sunburst finish, a two-tone design, or a chronograph dial with multiple subdials. Each additional color, texture, or complication adds time and materials to the process.

Brand and Parts Availability

Manufacturer-sourced replacement dials for brands like Rolex, Omega, or Cartier can be expensive and may have lead times. Generic or discontinued dials may be difficult to source at all, which sometimes makes refinishing the only practical option.

Watch Age and Rarity

Older watches may require more careful handling, and rare references may have unique dial configurations that complicate both refinishing and replacement. A specialist who has worked with the specific brand and era will produce better results than a generalist.

How to Choose the Right Option for Your Watch

The right path depends on your goals and the watch itself. Here is how to think through it:

If you want to preserve value on a collectible piece: Leave the original dial intact unless it is structurally failing. Even significant fading or patina is preferable to a refinished or replaced dial in most collector markets.

If you wear the watch daily and the appearance matters to you: Refinishing is usually the best balance of cost, turnaround, and result, provided the dial's base metal is in good condition.

If the dial has water damage, cracks, or structural issues: Replacement with a genuine manufacturer-sourced dial is typically the right move. Refinishing cannot fix what is broken underneath the surface.

If a previous refinishing job was botched: A genuine replacement dial will restore proper appearance and authenticity. Trying to refinish over poor earlier work rarely produces a satisfactory result.

If the watch has sentimental value but no significant market value: Go with whichever option makes the watch look and feel the way you want. The right choice is the one that keeps you wearing it.

What Happens During a Professional Dial Service

Whether you are having a dial refinished or replaced, the process at a qualified workshop follows a similar sequence. The watchmaker removes the movement from the case, separates the dial and hands, and assesses the condition of every component. If refinishing, the dial goes to a specialist who strips, recoats, reprints, and relumes the surface. If replacing, a compatible genuine dial is sourced, fitted, and aligned. In both cases, the watch is reassembled, tested for accuracy, and pressure tested if applicable before being returned.

At It's About Time Inc., every dial service is performed in-house by WOSTEP- and Swiss-certified watchmakers. We inspect the dial, explain what we find, and walk you through refinishing vs. replacement options before beginning any work. As a family-owned, watch-only repair and restoration shop in Johns Creek, we have been serving the Atlanta area since 2006.

Pro Tip

Ask your watchmaker whether they work with a dedicated dial refinishing specialist. Dial refinishing is a distinct trade from movement repair. The best workshops either have in-house dial restoration capability or a long-standing relationship with a proven refinishing house.

Brands We Commonly See for Dial Work

In our workshop, certain brands come in for dial services more than others. We regularly see faded dials on vintage Omega Seamasters and Constellations, moisture-related dial damage on Rolex sport models where gaskets were not replaced during prior service, loosened applied markers on TAG Heuer watches after impacts, and cosmetic wear on Cartier Tank and Santos dials. As an authorized service center for Omega, TAG Heuer, Cartier, Jaeger-LeCoultre, NOMOS, Baume & Mercier, Longines, RADO, and Tissot, It's About Time Inc. has the manufacturer training, tools, and genuine parts access to handle dial work to factory standards. Our watchmakers also hold certifications from Rolex, IWC, Panerai, and Audemars Piguet, giving us hands-on experience across a wide range of luxury references.

The Bottom Line on Dial Refinishing vs. Dial Replacement

  • Start with a professional inspection. The right recommendation depends on damage type, watch age, and your goals.
  • Refinishing works for surface-level wear: fading, discoloration, worn printing, degraded lume. The base metal must be structurally sound.
  • Replacement is the better option for water-corroded, cracked, or structurally compromised dials, and for watches with botched previous refinishing.
  • For vintage and collectible watches, originality matters more than appearance. A faded original dial is almost always more valuable than a refinished one.
  • Always use a workshop with brand-specific experience. Dial work is specialized, and the results vary significantly based on the skill of the person doing it.
  • Insist on genuine manufacturer-sourced parts for any replacement on a luxury watch. Aftermarket dials can compromise authenticity and future serviceability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between dial refinishing and dial replacement?+

Refinishing restores the existing dial; replacement removes it and installs a new one. With refinishing, a specialist strips the old finish, recoats the surface, and reprints the original markings, so the original dial is preserved in modified form. With replacement, the dial is swapped out entirely for a new component. The right option depends on the type and extent of damage to the dial.

Does refinishing a watch dial reduce its value?+

It can, especially on vintage or collectible watches where the original dial is a major driver of value. Collectors in those markets strongly prefer untouched original dials, even if faded or imperfect. For modern daily-wear watches with no significant collector premium, a well-done refinishing job can actually improve the watch's appeal and usability without meaningful value loss.

Can water-damaged watch dials be refinished?+

Sometimes, but only if the damage is limited to surface discoloration. Light moisture exposure that caused cosmetic changes may be correctable through refinishing. Severe water damage that caused oxidation, pitting, or corrosion into the base metal usually requires dial replacement instead. A qualified watchmaker can assess the dial's condition and recommend the right path. If you suspect water has entered your watch case, bring it in promptly to minimize further damage.

Should I refinish the dial on my vintage watch?+

In most collector market contexts, no. Original dials, even those showing significant age and patina, are typically the most valued component of a vintage watch, and refinishing can significantly reduce market value. The exception is when the dial is no longer legible or is structurally failing and the watch is intended for daily wear rather than collection. The model, era, and condition of your specific watch all factor into this decision, so consulting a qualified luxury watch specialist before proceeding is important.

How long does dial refinishing or replacement take?+

Refinishing often takes two to four weeks, though timelines vary significantly depending on the shop, dial complexity, and whether the work is handled in-house or sent to a dedicated refinishing specialist. Dial replacement turnaround depends on parts availability. In-stock genuine dials can be installed within days, while manufacturer-ordered parts for luxury brands may take several weeks. Your watchmaker should give you a clear timeline before work begins.

Can any watchmaker refinish a dial?+

No, dial refinishing is a distinct specialty that most general watchmakers do not perform themselves. It requires specific equipment, printing plates, paint formulations, and font libraries that go beyond standard movement repair tools. Most watchmakers send dial refinishing work to a dedicated specialist. When choosing a shop, ask whether they have in-house dial refinishing capability or a proven relationship with a specialist refinishing house.
